question: Shikamoo. tea zangu yanageuka manjano na madoa meusi. Nifanye nini?
answer: Brown, necrotic spots on leaves and dieback of young shoots indicate Tea Mosquito Bug (Helopeltis spp.). (1) Spray lambda-cyhalothrin at 1 ml/L OR quinalphos at 2 ml/L, targeting the new flush. (2) Maintain adequate shade (50-60%) — open areas suffer more damage. (3) Remove alternative host plants (especially guava, cashew) near the tea field. (4) Prune affected shoots and burn them. (5) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L as a repellent. Pre-harvest interval (plucking): lambda-cyhalothrin 7 days.
source: Sokoine University Extension Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Habari. Nina shida na oil palm. Majani yana yana wadudu wadogo kwenye majani. Nisaidie tafadhali.
answer: Yellowing patterns on oil palm indicate nutrient deficiency. (1) For nitrogen deficiency (uniform yellowing of older leaves): apply urea at 1-2 kg per tree per year, split into 2 applications. (2) For potassium deficiency (orange spotting on older leaves): apply muriate of potash at 2-3 kg per tree per year. (3) For magnesium deficiency (yellowing between veins of older leaves): apply kieserite at 0.5-1 kg per tree. (4) Apply empty fruit bunch (EFB) mulch at 60 t/ha around palms — it slowly releases nutrients. (5) Conduct a leaf analysis (take leaf #17 from 20 palms) to confirm which nutrients are deficient before large-scale fertiliser application.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Habari. Nina shida na amaranth. Majani yana yana wadudu wadogo kwenye majani. Nisaidie tafadhali.
answer: White powdery coating on leaves indicates powdery mildew (Erysiphales). It reduces photosynthesis and weakens plants. (1) Spray sulfur-based fungicide (micronized sulfur at 3 g/L) or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) every 7 days. (2) Improve air circulation by wider spacing and removing excess foliage. (3) Avoid overhead irrigation — water at the base of plants. (4) Spray a solution of 1 part milk to 9 parts water — milk proteins have antifungal properties effective against powdery mildew. Apply weekly. (5) Remove and burn heavily infected leaves. Pre-harvest interval for sulfur: 1 day.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Habari. Nina shida na cabbage. Majani yana hayakui vizuri, majani yanakauka. Nisaidie tafadhali.
answer: V-shaped yellow lesions at leaf margins with blackened veins indicate black rot (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris). (1) Remove and destroy affected plants — the bacteria spread through water. (2) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L to protect remaining plants. (3) Use hot-water treated seed (50°C for 25 minutes) for the next planting. (4) Never work in the field when plants are wet. (5) Rotate with non-crucifer crops (maize, cowpea) for 3-4 years. (6) Control weeds in the cabbage family (wild mustard, shepherd's purse) that harbour the bacteria.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Habari. Nina shida na watermelon. Majani yana yanageuka manjano na madoa meusi. Nisaidie tafadhali.
answer: Small black or pale green insects clustered on stems and young growth are aphids. They suck sap and can transmit viruses. (1) Spray insecticidal soap (5 ml liquid soap in 1 L water) directly on the insects every 3 days. (2) Strong water spray can dislodge light infestations. (3) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L. (4) Encourage natural enemies: ladybirds (ladybugs), lacewings, and hoverflies — plant marigold or coriander near watermelon to attract them. (5) If infestation is severe and ants are present (ants farm aphids), apply imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L. Remove ants with a sticky barrier around plant stems first.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Habari. Nina shida na cashew. Majani yana yana wadudu wadogo kwenye majani. Nisaidie tafadhali.
answer: Brown, necrotic spots on leaves and dieback of young shoots indicate Tea Mosquito Bug (Helopeltis spp.). (1) Spray lambda-cyhalothrin at 1 ml/L OR quinalphos at 2 ml/L, targeting the new flush. (2) Maintain adequate shade (50-60%) — open areas suffer more damage. (3) Remove alternative host plants (especially guava, cashew) near the tea field. (4) Prune affected shoots and burn them. (5) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L as a repellent. Pre-harvest interval (plucking): lambda-cyhalothrin 7 days.
source: ICIPE Integrated Pest Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Habari. Nina shida na cassava. Majani yana hayakui vizuri, majani yanakauka. Nisaidie tafadhali.
answer: Green mites (Mononychellus tanajoa) cause stippling and leaf distortion on cassava. (1) Spray water forcefully on the underside of leaves to dislodge mites. (2) Apply sulfur-based miticide at 2 g/L, or micronized sulfur dust at 15 kg/ha during dry weather. (3) Avoid pyrethroid insecticides — they kill predatory mites that control this pest. (4) Maintain plant health with adequate potassium fertiliser (apply muriate of potash at 60 kg/ha). (5) Introduce Typhlodromalus aripo predatory mites available from IITA if the problem recurs across multiple seasons.
source: KALRO Diagnostic Manual; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Habari. Nina shida na maize. Majani yana hayakui vizuri, majani yanakauka. Nisaidie tafadhali.
answer: Holes in stems and 'dead hearts' (withered central shoot) indicate stem borers (Busseola fusca / Chilo partellus). (1) Pull out and destroy dead heart plants — larvae inside can spread to healthy plants. (2) Apply crushed neem leaves (1 kg/10 L water, steep 24 hours) into the leaf whorl — repeat weekly. (3) Apply carbofuran 3G granules at 0.75 kg a.i./ha into the whorl at knee-height stage. (4) After harvest, cut stubble to ground level and bury or burn crop residues to kill overwintering larvae. (5) Rotate with legumes (cowpea, groundnut) to break the pest cycle.
source: Sokoine University Extension Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Shikamoo. tomato zangu yana wadudu wadogo kwenye majani. Nifanye nini?
answer: Concentric ring spots on older leaves indicate early blight (Alternaria solani). (1) Remove affected lower leaves and burn them. (2) Spray chlorothalonil at 2 g/L or mancozeb at 2.5 g/L every 7-10 days. (3) Apply 2-3 cm of organic mulch to prevent soil splash. (4) Ensure adequate potassium — apply 100 kg/ha muriate of potash. (5) Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (maize, beans) for 2-3 years. (6) Stake plants to keep foliage off the ground. Pre-harvest interval: chlorothalonil 7 days.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Habari. Nina shida na rice. Majani yana yana wadudu wadogo kwenye majani. Nisaidie tafadhali.
answer: Grey-whitish lesions on leaves with brown borders indicate rice blast (Magnaporthe grisea). This is the most destructive rice disease worldwide. (1) Avoid excessive nitrogen — limit urea to 60 kg/ha in blast-prone areas and split into 3 doses. (2) Spray tricyclazole at 0.6 g/L or isoprothiolane at 1 ml/L at first sign and repeat after 10-14 days. (3) Maintain 2-3 cm of standing water in the field; intermittent drying stresses plants and increases susceptibility. (4) Plant resistant varieties: NERICA 4, ARICA 3, or IR64. (5) Burn infected straw after harvest — the fungus survives in crop residue.
source: TARI Crop Management Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Shikamoo. cowpea zangu yanageuka manjano na madoa meusi. Nifanye nini?
answer: Holes in pods with frass (insect droppings) indicate pod borer (Maruca vitrata / Helicoverpa armigera). (1) Hand-pick visible caterpillars at dawn. (2) Spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) at 2 g/L in the evening — it degrades in sunlight. (3) Apply neem seed kernel extract (50 g/L, soak 12 hrs, strain) weekly. (4) Plant early-maturing varieties to escape peak pest pressure. (5) Install pheromone traps (1 per 0.1 ha) to monitor moth flights. (6) After harvest, deep-plough (20-25 cm) to expose pupae to sunlight and birds. Pre-harvest interval for Bt: 0 days (safe up to harvest day).
source: TARI Crop Management Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Habari. Nina shida na mango. Majani yana yanageuka manjano na madoa meusi. Nisaidie tafadhali.
answer: Soft spots on fruit with small puncture marks and larvae (maggots) inside indicate fruit fly (Bactrocera / Ceratitis spp.). (1) Collect ALL fallen and infested fruit daily — place them in a sealed black plastic bag and leave in the sun for 7 days to kill larvae. (2) Use methyl eugenol pheromone traps (1 trap per 0.1 ha). (3) Apply GF-120 (Spinosad-based fruit fly bait) as spot sprays on a small patch of leaves — do NOT spray the fruit. (4) Bag individual fruits with paper bags when they reach half-size. (5) Plough the soil under the tree canopy to expose pupae. (6) NEVER use unapproved systemic insecticides on fruit crops.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Shikamoo. groundnut zangu hayakui vizuri, majani yanakauka. Nifanye nini?
answer: Brown spots on groundnut leaves indicate leaf spot disease (Cercospora / Alternaria spp.). (1) Remove and destroy affected leaves. (2) Spray mancozeb at 2.5 g/L OR copper oxychloride at 3 g/L every 10-14 days. (3) Improve air circulation through wider spacing. (4) Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet. (5) Apply well-rotted compost at 2 t/ha to boost plant immunity. (6) Rotate with non-host crops for 2 seasons.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Shikamoo. yam zangu hayakui vizuri, majani yanakauka. Nifanye nini?
answer: Soft, watery rot of tubers during storage indicates tuber rot caused by fungi or bacteria. (1) Sort tubers carefully DURING harvest — any cut, bruised, or insect-damaged tuber must be consumed immediately or processed, not stored. (2) Cure tubers by spreading them in a well-ventilated shaded area for 2-3 days, then dust cut surfaces with wood ash. (3) Store in a cool, dry, ventilated place — yam barns with vertical stacking work well. (4) Never store in sealed plastic bags — they trap moisture. (5) Inspect stored tubers weekly and remove any showing signs of rot. (6) For loose tubers, dust with Trichoderma powder (2 g per tuber) before storage.
source: TARI Crop Management Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Shikamoo. cocoa zangu hayakui vizuri, majani yanakauka. Nifanye nini?
answer: Black, rotting pods covered with whitish fungal growth indicate black pod disease (Phytophthora megakarya / P. palmivora) — the most damaging disease of cocoa. (1) Remove ALL infected pods immediately — they produce spores that spread to healthy pods. Bury them 30 cm deep away from the farm. (2) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L OR metalaxyl + copper at 2 g/L on ALL pods every 3 weeks during the rainy season. (3) Prune shade trees — too much shade (over 50%) creates high humidity that favours the disease. (4) Harvest pods as soon as they show yellow colour — do NOT let them over-ripen on the tree. Pre-harvest interval for copper: 14 days.
source: KALRO Diagnostic Manual; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Shikamoo. plantain zangu yanageuka manjano na madoa meusi. Nifanye nini?
answer: Upright, crowded leaves with a 'bunchy' appearance and dark green streaking on petioles indicate Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV) transmitted by the banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa). There is NO cure. (1) Uproot and destroy the entire plant including the corm — bury or burn it. (2) Control the aphid vector by spraying imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L on all surrounding plants. (3) Never use suckers from an affected field for new plantings. (4) Use tissue-culture plantlets — they are guaranteed virus-free. (5) Contact your agricultural extension office to report BBTV — it is a notifiable disease in most countries. (6) Quarantine any new planting material for 4 weeks.
source: TARI Crop Management Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: sweet potato ki fasal mein peele ho rahe hain aur kaale dhabbe hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Stunted growth, yellowing, swollen root galls (knots), and wilting despite moist soil indicate root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.). (1) There is no curative chemical treatment. (2) Incorporate fresh neem leaves or neem cake at 500 kg/ha into the soil 2 weeks before the next planting. (3) Solarize the soil with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks. (4) Plant marigold (Tagetes erecta) as a trap crop — its roots release natural nematicides. (5) Rotate with maize, sorghum, or millet for 2-3 seasons — these are non-hosts. (6) Apply well-composted manure at 5 t/ha; the microbial activity suppresses nematodes.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: onion ki fasal mein peele ho rahe hain aur kaale dhabbe hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Purple-brown oval lesions on leaves and flower stalks indicate purple blotch (Alternaria porri). (1) Spray mancozeb at 2.5 g/L OR iprodione at 1.5 g/L every 10 days. (2) Avoid excessive nitrogen — apply NPK 10-10-20 rather than high-nitrogen fertilisers. (3) Ensure good field drainage. (4) Rotate with non-allium crops for 3 years. (5) Harvest bulbs only when necks are fully dry; cure properly before storage. Pre-harvest interval: mancozeb 7 days.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere pepper ki pattiyan patton par chhote keede hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Silvery streaks on leaves and distorted young growth indicate thrips. (1) Spray spinosad at 0.3 ml/L or neem oil at 5 ml/L every 5 days. (2) Use blue sticky traps (thrips are more attracted to blue than yellow), 1 trap per 5 m². (3) Remove weeds from around the field — they serve as alternative hosts. (4) Maintain adequate soil moisture — drought stressed plants are more vulnerable. (5) For heavy infestations, apply imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L as a soil drench. Pre-harvest interval: spinosad 3 days.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: okra ki fasal mein peele ho rahe hain aur kaale dhabbe hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Holes in developing pods with black frass indicate fruit borer (Earias spp. / Helicoverpa armigera). (1) Hand-pick caterpillars at dawn. (2) Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) at 2 g/L in the evening every 7 days. (3) Apply neem seed kernel extract (50 g/L). (4) Install pheromone traps at 5 traps/ha. (5) Plant trap crop: maize rows around okra to attract borers away. (6) Remove crop residues after harvest and deep-plough.
source: ICAR Crop Production Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: millet ki fasal mein theek se nahi badh raha, pattiyan sookh rahi hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Discoloured, mouldy grain heads indicate grain mold caused by a complex of fungi (Fusarium, Curvularia, Alternaria). (1) Harvest at the RIGHT maturity — delayed harvest increases mold. Grain should be hard and not produce milky liquid when pressed. (2) Dry grains immediately to 12-13% moisture. Use raised drying racks. (3) Sort and discard all discoloured grains before storage. (4) Store in hermetic (PICS) bags or clean metal containers. (5) For the next season, plant mold-tolerant varieties (e.g., ICSV series for sorghum). (6) NEVER consume or feed visibly mouldy grain — it may contain mycotoxins.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere coffee ki pattiyan peele ho rahe hain aur kaale dhabbe hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Dark, sunken lesions on green berries that turn black and drop indicate Coffee Berry Disease (Colletotrichum kahawae). (1) Spray copper oxychloride at 5 g/L on the developing berries at 4, 8, and 12 weeks after flowering. (2) Prune to maintain an open canopy — this reduces humidity and spore dispersal. (3) Strip and burn all mummified berries remaining on branches after harvest. (4) Apply 2 t/ha of well-rotted compost to improve tree vigour. (5) Plant resistant varieties: Ruiru 11 or Batian (available in Kenya). Pre-harvest interval for copper: 21 days.
source: ICAR Crop Production Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere cotton ki pattiyan patton par chhote keede hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Yellowing leaf margins that curl downward ('hopper burn') indicate jassids (Amrasca biguttula). (1) Spray imidacloprid at 0.3 ml/L OR acetamiprid at 0.2 g/L. (2) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L as a repellent. (3) Maintain adequate soil moisture — drought-stressed crops are more attractive to jassids. (4) Use yellow sticky traps (1 per 2 m²). (5) Plant resistant varieties with hairy leaves (hirsutum-type cotton). Pre-harvest interval for imidacloprid: 21 days.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal; reviewed agricultural literature

question: tea ki fasal mein peele ho rahe hain aur kaale dhabbe hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Translucent blisters on young leaves that turn brown and break indicate Blister Blight (Exobasidium vexans). (1) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L OR hexaconazole at 1 ml/L every 7-10 days during monsoon. (2) Maintain adequate shade (50-60%) — direct sunlight makes blister blight worse. (3) Pluck and destroy all affected leaves. (4) Apply balanced NPK (YTD or similar tea mixture) at recommended rates to maintain bush health. (5) Prune to maintain plucking table height — do NOT allow bushes to become too tall and dense. Pre-plucking interval: copper 7 days.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: oil palm ki fasal mein patton par chhote keede hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: V-shaped cuts in fronds and holes at the crown indicate rhinoceros beetle (Oryctes rhinoceros). (1) Hand-pick beetles at night using a torch — they are large and easy to spot. (2) Remove and destroy rotting trunks and compost heaps near the plantation — these are breeding sites. (3) Apply naphthalene balls (mothballs, 2-3 per palm) in the leaf axils. (4) Use Oryctes NudiVirus (available from research stations) — it infects and kills larvae. (5) Fill the crown with a mixture of sand + neem cake (50:50) to deter egg-laying. (6) For large plantations, install pheromone traps (ethyl 4-methyloctanoate) at 1 trap/ha.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere cabbage ki pattiyan patton par chhote keede hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Seedlings cut at ground level overnight indicate cutworm (Agrotis spp.). (1) Hand-pick cutworms from the soil surface at night using a torch — they hide in the top 2-3 cm of soil during the day and come up to feed at night. (2) Place collars around seedlings: cut the bottom from a plastic cup or use a cardboard tube pushed 2 cm into the soil. (3) Apply neem cake at 50 g per square metre around plants — it deters egg-laying. (4) Sprinkle wood ash in a ring around each plant. (5) Plough the field 2-3 weeks before planting to expose larvae to birds.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal; reviewed agricultural literature

question: cashew ki fasal mein theek se nahi badh raha, pattiyan sookh rahi hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Dark, sunken lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit indicate anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.). (1) Remove and destroy all infected plant parts — do NOT compost them. (4) Apply 2-3 cm of organic mulch to prevent rain splash. (5) For the next season, use certified disease-free seed and practice 3-year crop rotation with cereals. Pre-harvest interval: 7-14 days depending on the product.

question: Namaste. Mere cassava ki pattiyan patton par chhote keede hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?

question: maize ki fasal mein theek se nahi badh raha, pattiyan sookh rahi hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Chlorotic streaks following leaf veins indicate Maize Streak Virus transmitted by leafhoppers (Cicadulina spp.). There is no cure. (1) Remove and destroy all affected plants immediately. (2) Plant early at the onset of rains to avoid peak leafhopper populations. (3) Use streak-resistant hybrids: ZM 623, SC 627, or WH 505. (4) Do not plant maize near irrigated vegetable fields, which harbor leafhoppers year-round. (5) Apply carbofuran granules at 1.5 kg a.i./ha to the soil at planting to control early-season vectors. (6) Save seed only from completely disease-free plants.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: tomato ki fasal mein theek se nahi badh raha, pattiyan sookh rahi hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Dark spots on leaves with white fungal growth on the underside and rotting fruit indicate late blight (Phytophthora infestans). This disease can destroy a field within DAYS in wet weather. (1) Spray mancozeb (2.5 g/L) OR metalaxyl-M + mancozeb (Ridomil Gold) at 2 g/L, alternating every 7 days. (2) Improve staking and pruning so leaves don't touch soil. (3) NEVER work in the field when leaves are wet. (4) Remove and bury infected plant material away from the field. (5) Plant resistant varieties like Rio Grande or Roma VF. (6) Apply mulch to reduce rain splash. Pre-harvest interval for mancozeb: 5 days.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere rice ki pattiyan patton par chhote keede hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Bronze-orange discolouration of older leaves ("bronzing") indicates iron toxicity, common in waterlogged, acidic soils. (1) Drain the field for 3-5 days to aerate the soil — this allows iron to precipitate out of the soil solution. (2) Apply lime (2-4 t/ha) to raise soil pH above 5.0. (3) Use NPK 15-15-15 fertiliser rather than single-nutrient fertilisers — potassium helps reduce iron uptake. (4) Plant tolerant varieties: NERICA-L series or TOX 4004. (5) In the next season, avoid continuous flooding of young seedlings; use alternate wetting and drying irrigation.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere mango ki pattiyan patton par chhote keede hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Dark bore holes on fruit and larvae inside the seed indicate mango seed weevil (Sternochetus mangiferae). The adult lays eggs on developing fruit and larvae tunnel into the seed. (1) Collect and destroy ALL fallen fruit and seeds — the weevil completes its lifecycle in the seed. (2) Spray lambda-cyhalothrin at 1 ml/L when fruit are marble-sized (2-3 cm). Repeat after 21 days. (3) Maintain orchard hygiene: remove and burn fallen leaves and debris. (4) Band tree trunks with sticky bands to trap weevils climbing up. (5) Harvest fruit slightly early (mature green stage) and store away from orchards.
source: ICAR Crop Production Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: yam ki fasal mein theek se nahi badh raha, pattiyan sookh rahi hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Holes in leaves and tubers indicate yam beetle (Heteroligus spp.). (1) Hand-pick beetles at night when they are active and visible with a torch. (2) Apply carbofuran granules at 1.0 kg a.i./ha to the soil around the mounds at planting. (3) Delay planting until after the first heavy rains when beetle populations naturally decline. (4) Hill up (re-mound) yam mounds to expose beetles and their eggs. (5) Plant resistant varieties: Dioscorea rotundata cultivars show better tolerance. (6) After harvest, deep-plough to expose overwintering beetles to predators.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: cocoa ki fasal mein theek se nahi badh raha, pattiyan sookh rahi hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Sunken, black lesions on young shoots and pods indicate mirids/capsids (Sahlbergella singularis). (1) Spray imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L OR bifenthrin at 1 ml/L, targeting the canopy thoroughly. (2) Remove and burn heavily damaged shoots and pods. (3) Maintain adequate canopy shade — mirids prefer open, exposed canopies. (4) Avoid excessive pruning that exposes the tree interior. (5) Monitor weekly with a beating tray or by tapping branches over a white cloth to count insects. Treat when you find >4 mirids per 10 taps.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: plantain ki fasal mein theek se nahi badh raha, pattiyan sookh rahi hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Stunted growth, yellowing, swollen root galls (knots), and wilting despite moist soil indicate root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.). (1) There is no curative chemical treatment. (2) Incorporate fresh neem leaves or neem cake at 500 kg/ha into the soil 2 weeks before the next planting. (3) Solarize the soil with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks. (4) Plant marigold (Tagetes erecta) as a trap crop — its roots release natural nematicides. (5) Rotate with maize, sorghum, or millet for 2-3 seasons — these are non-hosts. (6) Apply well-composted manure at 5 t/ha; the microbial activity suppresses nematodes.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere sorghum ki pattiyan theek se nahi badh raha, pattiyan sookh rahi hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Small pink-purple flowering weeds attached to the roots of your sorghum are Striga (witchweed). Each plant produces 50,000+ seeds that persist in soil for 15+ years. (1) Hand-pull ALL Striga plants BEFORE they flower — pull and burn them. (2) Do NOT plant sorghum in the same field next season — rotate with groundnut or cowpea which trigger Striga seed germination but are not parasitised ('suicidal germination'). (3) Apply imazapyr-resistant maize varieties (StrigAway / IR-maize) coated with herbicide at planting. (4) Apply 2 t/ha of well-composted farmyard manure — it improves soil fertility and reduces Striga emergence. (5) Deep-plough after harvest to bury seeds below the germination zone.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal; reviewed agricultural literature

question: banana ki fasal mein peele ho rahe hain aur kaale dhabbe hain dikh raha hai. Kya upay hai?
answer: Upright, crowded leaves with a 'bunchy' appearance and dark green streaking on petioles indicate Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV) transmitted by the banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa). There is NO cure. (1) Uproot and destroy the entire plant including the corm — bury or burn it. (2) Control the aphid vector by spraying imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L on all surrounding plants. (3) Never use suckers from an affected field for new plantings. (4) Use tissue-culture plantlets — they are guaranteed virus-free. (5) Contact your agricultural extension office to report BBTV — it is a notifiable disease in most countries. (6) Quarantine any new planting material for 4 weeks.
source: ICAR Crop Production Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere sweet potato ki pattiyan patton par chhote keede hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Tunnels in tubers with a bitter taste and smell indicate sweet potato weevil (Cylas spp.). (1) Hill up (mound) soil around the base of plants to cover exposed roots — weevils enter through soil cracks. (2) Remove and destroy all infested tubers and debris after harvest. (3) Rotate land — do NOT plant sweet potato in the same field for 2 years. (4) Apply neem cake at 200 kg/ha at planting. (5) Irrigate regularly to prevent soil cracking. (6) Use early-maturing varieties (3-4 months) and harvest immediately at maturity — delayed harvest increases weevil damage.
source: ICAR Crop Production Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere onion ki pattiyan peele ho rahe hain aur kaale dhabbe hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Pale yellow patches on upper leaf surface with grey-purple fuzz underneath indicate downy mildew (Peronospora spp.). (1) Spray metalaxyl-M + mancozeb at 2 g/L OR phosphorous acid at 3 ml/L every 7-10 days. (2) Improve field drainage and air circulation. (3) Avoid overhead irrigation in the evening — water early morning instead. (4) Remove crop debris after harvest. (5) Use disease-free seed for the next planting. (6) For onion, cure bulbs properly (7-10 days in sun) before storage.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere pepper ki pattiyan peele ho rahe hain aur kaale dhabbe hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Sudden wilting of green plants with no leaf yellowing indicates bacterial wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum). Cut the stem — if it oozes a milky bacterial stream in water, it's confirmed. There is NO chemical cure. (1) Uproot and burn affected plants. (2) Raise soil pH to 6.0-6.5 by applying lime (2 t/ha). (3) Graft pepper onto resistant rootstocks (e.g., EG 203 eggplant rootstock). (4) Rotate with maize or sorghum for 3-4 years — the bacteria survive in soil. (5) Solarize soil before the next planting. (6) Never plant pepper after tomato, potato, or eggplant.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere okra ki pattiyan patton par chhote keede hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: White powdery coating on leaves indicates powdery mildew (Erysiphales). It reduces photosynthesis and weakens plants. (1) Spray sulfur-based fungicide (micronized sulfur at 3 g/L) or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) every 7 days. (2) Improve air circulation by wider spacing and removing excess foliage. (3) Avoid overhead irrigation — water at the base of plants. (4) Spray a solution of 1 part milk to 9 parts water — milk proteins have antifungal properties effective against powdery mildew. Apply weekly. (5) Remove and burn heavily infected leaves. Pre-harvest interval for sulfur: 1 day.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere millet ki pattiyan theek se nahi badh raha, pattiyan sookh rahi hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Discoloured, mouldy grain heads indicate grain mold caused by a complex of fungi (Fusarium, Curvularia, Alternaria). (1) Harvest at the RIGHT maturity — delayed harvest increases mold. Grain should be hard and not produce milky liquid when pressed. (2) Dry grains immediately to 12-13% moisture. Use raised drying racks. (3) Sort and discard all discoloured grains before storage. (4) Store in hermetic (PICS) bags or clean metal containers. (5) For the next season, plant mold-tolerant varieties (e.g., ICSV series for sorghum). (6) NEVER consume or feed visibly mouldy grain — it may contain mycotoxins.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere coffee ki pattiyan patton par chhote keede hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Soft, foul-smelling roots indicate root rot caused by soil fungi (Pythium/Phytophthora). (1) Stop watering immediately — wet soil accelerates the rot. (2) Improve drainage by creating raised beds 30 cm high. (3) Remove and destroy all affected plants. (4) Drench the remaining soil with Trichoderma viride at 2.5 kg/ha mixed with 50 kg of well-rotted compost. (5) For the next planting season, solarize the soil by covering beds with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks during the hottest months. (6) Rotate coffee with maize or sorghum for at least 2 seasons before replanting.
source: ICAR Crop Production Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Namaste. Mere cotton ki pattiyan peele ho rahe hain aur kaale dhabbe hain ho rahi hain. Kya karna chahiye?
answer: Angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown indicate bacterial blight (Xanthomonas spp.). (1) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L + streptomycin at 0.3 g/L at first sign. (2) Avoid working in the field when plants are wet — bacteria spread through water. (3) Use only acid-delinted, certified seed. (4) Rotate with maize or sorghum for 2-3 years. (5) Remove and burn all crop residues after harvest. (6) Avoid excessive nitrogen which promotes lush, susceptible growth.
source: Punjab Agricultural University Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my tea are are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Silvery streaks on leaves and distorted young growth indicate thrips. (1) Spray spinosad at 0.3 ml/L or neem oil at 5 ml/L every 5 days. (2) Use blue sticky traps (thrips are more attracted to blue than yellow), 1 trap per 5 m². (3) Remove weeds from around the field — they serve as alternative hosts. (4) Maintain adequate soil moisture — drought stressed plants are more vulnerable. (5) For heavy infestations, apply imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L as a soil drench. Pre-harvest interval: spinosad 3 days.
source: CIAT Agricultural Advisory; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Good morning. My oil palm plants have small insects clustered on them. I've tried a few things but it's getting worse. What should I do?
answer: Multiple factors could cause your crop's symptoms. My recommendation: take a sample of the affected leaves to your nearest agricultural extension office. An extension officer can examine it in person and give you an accurate diagnosis. Don't delay — crop diseases spread quickly.
source: CSIR-SARI Production Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my cabbage are have small insects clustered on them. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Small holes in leaves and green caterpillars that wriggle violently when disturbed indicate diamondback moth (Plutella xylostella). (1) Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis var. kurstaki) at 2 g/L every 7 days — it targets caterpillars only. (2) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L. (3) Use pheromone traps to monitor moth populations. (4) Rotate insecticide groups — diamondback moth rapidly develops resistance. Alternate Bt with spinosad at 0.3 ml/L. (5) Remove and destroy crop residues after harvest. (6) Plant trap crop: Indian mustard attracts moths away from cabbage.

question: Hello. The leaves on my watermelon are have small insects clustered on them. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Small black or pale green insects clustered on stems and young growth are aphids. They suck sap and can transmit viruses. (1) Spray insecticidal soap (5 ml liquid soap in 1 L water) directly on the insects every 3 days. (2) Strong water spray can dislodge light infestations. (3) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L. (4) Encourage natural enemies: ladybirds (ladybugs), lacewings, and hoverflies — plant marigold or coriander near watermelon to attract them. (5) If infestation is severe and ants are present (ants farm aphids), apply imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L. Remove ants with a sticky barrier around plant stems first.
source: CSIR-SARI Production Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Good morning. My cashew plants are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I've tried a few things but it's getting worse. What should I do?
answer: Brown, necrotic spots on leaves and dieback of young shoots indicate Tea Mosquito Bug (Helopeltis spp.). (1) Spray lambda-cyhalothrin at 1 ml/L OR quinalphos at 2 ml/L, targeting the new flush. (2) Maintain adequate shade (50-60%) — open areas suffer more damage. (3) Remove alternative host plants (especially guava, cashew) near the tea field. (4) Prune affected shoots and burn them. (5) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L as a repellent. Pre-harvest interval (plucking): lambda-cyhalothrin 7 days.
source: CIMMYT Southern Africa Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my maize are have small insects clustered on them. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Chlorotic streaks following leaf veins indicate Maize Streak Virus transmitted by leafhoppers (Cicadulina spp.). There is no cure. (1) Remove and destroy all affected plants immediately. (2) Plant early at the onset of rains to avoid peak leafhopper populations. (3) Use streak-resistant hybrids: ZM 623, SC 627, or WH 505. (4) Do not plant maize near irrigated vegetable fields, which harbor leafhoppers year-round. (5) Apply carbofuran granules at 1.5 kg a.i./ha to the soil at planting to control early-season vectors. (6) Save seed only from completely disease-free plants.
source: CIAT Agricultural Advisory; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my tomato are are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Fine webbing and yellow stippling on leaves indicate spider mites (Tetranychus spp.), which thrive in hot, dry conditions. (1) Spray the underside of leaves with a strong jet of water every 3 days to dislodge mites and break webbing. (2) Apply micronized sulfur at 3 g/L or abamectin at 0.5 ml/L. (3) Avoid pyrethroids and broad-spectrum insecticides — they kill predatory mites and trigger mite explosions. (4) Increase humidity around plants by mulching and watering the ground (not leaves) in the morning. (5) For heavy infestation, release Phytoseiulus persimilis predatory mites — 10/m².
source: CIMMYT Southern Africa Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Good morning. My rice plants are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I've tried a few things but it's getting worse. What should I do?
answer: Proper water management directly affects rice yield and disease pressure. (1) Maintain 2-3 cm of standing water from tillering until grain filling, then drain the field 1-2 weeks before harvest. (2) If water is limited, use alternate wetting and drying: flood the field to 5 cm, let it drop to 15 cm below the soil surface, then re-flood. (3) Never let the soil crack — this damages roots. (4) In rainfed systems, construct contour bunds and bund the field edges to retain rainfall. (5) Apply 5 cm of rice straw mulch between rows to reduce evaporation by 30-40%.
source: KALRO Diagnostic Manual; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my mango are are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Dark bore holes on fruit and larvae inside the seed indicate mango seed weevil (Sternochetus mangiferae). The adult lays eggs on developing fruit and larvae tunnel into the seed. (1) Collect and destroy ALL fallen fruit and seeds — the weevil completes its lifecycle in the seed. (2) Spray lambda-cyhalothrin at 1 ml/L when fruit are marble-sized (2-3 cm). Repeat after 21 days. (3) Maintain orchard hygiene: remove and burn fallen leaves and debris. (4) Band tree trunks with sticky bands to trap weevils climbing up. (5) Harvest fruit slightly early (mature green stage) and store away from orchards.

question: Good morning. My cocoa plants are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I've tried a few things but it's getting worse. What should I do?
answer: Holes in pods with frass (insect droppings) indicate pod borer (Maruca vitrata / Helicoverpa armigera). (1) Hand-pick visible caterpillars at dawn. (2) Spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) at 2 g/L in the evening — it degrades in sunlight. (3) Apply neem seed kernel extract (50 g/L, soak 12 hrs, strain) weekly. (4) Plant early-maturing varieties to escape peak pest pressure. (5) Install pheromone traps (1 per 0.1 ha) to monitor moth flights. (6) After harvest, deep-plough (20-25 cm) to expose pupae to sunlight and birds. Pre-harvest interval for Bt: 0 days (safe up to harvest day).
source: CIAT Agricultural Advisory; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my plantain are are turning yellow with dark spots. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Holes at the base of the pseudostem and wilting plants indicate banana/plantain weevil borer (Cosmopolites sordidus). (1) Set up pseudostem traps: cut a 30 cm piece of harvested stem, split it lengthwise, and place it cut-side down near the plant. Check and destroy trapped weevils every 2 days. (2) Apply neem cake at 100 g per plant around the base. (3) Remove old, harvested stems at ground level — they are breeding sites. (4) For heavy infestation, drench the soil around the base with chlorpyrifos at 2 ml/L (wear gloves and avoid runoff into water sources). (5) Use clean, weevil-free suckers for the next planting.
source: MOFA Extension Manual; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Good morning. My sweet potato plants have small insects clustered on them. I've tried a few things but it's getting worse. What should I do?
answer: Distorted, mottled leaves and stunted growth on sweet potato indicate a viral infection, often transmitted by aphids or whiteflies. (1) Remove and destroy affected plants — viruses cannot be cured. (2) Control the insect vectors with neem oil (5 ml/L) or imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L. (3) Use only certified virus-free planting material (vine cuttings or slips). (4) Remove weeds (especially morning glory and other Ipomoea species) that harbour the virus. (5) Plant a barrier crop (maize or sorghum) to disrupt insect movement into the field. (6) Wash hands and tools before handling healthy plants.
source: Sokoine University Extension Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my onion are are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Wilting seedlings with small white maggots in the bulb indicate onion maggot (Delia antiqua). (1) Remove and destroy infested plants. (2) Apply spinosad-based bait at 2 g/m² around the base of plants. (3) Use floating row covers (insect netting) over nursery beds. (4) Apply neem cake at 500 kg/ha to the soil before planting — it repels egg-laying flies. (5) Deep-plough after harvest to expose pupae. (6) Rotate with non-allium crops for 3 years.
source: ICIPE Integrated Pest Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my pepper are are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Brown spots on pepper leaves indicate leaf spot disease (Cercospora / Alternaria spp.). (1) Remove and destroy affected leaves. (2) Spray mancozeb at 2.5 g/L OR copper oxychloride at 3 g/L every 10-14 days. (3) Improve air circulation through wider spacing. (4) Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet. (5) Apply well-rotted compost at 2 t/ha to boost plant immunity. (6) Rotate with non-host crops for 2 seasons.
source: ICIPE Integrated Pest Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Good morning. My millet plants are turning yellow with dark spots. I've tried a few things but it's getting worse. What should I do?
answer: Holes in stems and 'dead hearts' (withered central shoot) indicate stem borers (Busseola fusca / Chilo partellus). (1) Pull out and destroy dead heart plants — larvae inside can spread to healthy plants. (2) Apply crushed neem leaves (1 kg/10 L water, steep 24 hours) into the leaf whorl — repeat weekly. (3) Apply carbofuran 3G granules at 0.75 kg a.i./ha into the whorl at knee-height stage. (4) After harvest, cut stubble to ground level and bury or burn crop residues to kill overwintering larvae. (5) Rotate with legumes (cowpea, groundnut) to break the pest cycle.
source: KALRO Diagnostic Manual; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my coffee are are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Orange-yellow powdery pustules on the underside of leaves indicate Coffee Leaf Rust (Hemileia vastatrix). (1) Spray copper oxychloride at 5 g/L OR propiconazole at 1 ml/L at the first sign and repeat every 3-4 weeks during the rainy season. (2) Maintain adequate shade (30-40%) to reduce disease pressure. (3) Apply balanced NPK 20-10-10 at 200 kg/ha after pruning to strengthen trees. (4) Prune to open the canopy. (5) Plant resistant varieties: Castillo, Batian, or Ruiru 11.
source: CIAT Agricultural Advisory; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my cotton are have small insects clustered on them. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Yellowing leaves that wilt during the day and internal stem browning indicate Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum). Once a plant shows symptoms, it cannot be saved. (1) Uproot and burn the affected plant with its root ball — do NOT compost. (2) Drench the planting hole with Trichoderma viride (10 g/L) + lime (50 g/hole). (3) Do NOT plant susceptible crops in that spot for 3-4 years — rotate with maize or rice. (4) Solarize the soil during the hottest months. (5) Use resistant varieties (FHIA series for banana). (6) Always use tissue-culture plantlets or certified disease-free suckers for new plantings — the fungus persists in infected planting material.
source: DARS Extension Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my tea are are turning yellow with dark spots. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Translucent blisters on young leaves that turn brown and break indicate Blister Blight (Exobasidium vexans). (1) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L OR hexaconazole at 1 ml/L every 7-10 days during monsoon. (2) Maintain adequate shade (50-60%) — direct sunlight makes blister blight worse. (3) Pluck and destroy all affected leaves. (4) Apply balanced NPK (YTD or similar tea mixture) at recommended rates to maintain bush health. (5) Prune to maintain plucking table height — do NOT allow bushes to become too tall and dense. Pre-plucking interval: copper 7 days.
source: KALRO Diagnostic Manual; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Good morning. My cabbage plants are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I've tried a few things but it's getting worse. What should I do?
answer: Small black or pale green insects clustered on stems and young growth are aphids. They suck sap and can transmit viruses. (1) Spray insecticidal soap (5 ml liquid soap in 1 L water) directly on the insects every 3 days. (2) Strong water spray can dislodge light infestations. (3) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L. (4) Encourage natural enemies: ladybirds (ladybugs), lacewings, and hoverflies — plant marigold or coriander near cabbage to attract them. (5) If infestation is severe and ants are present (ants farm aphids), apply imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L. Remove ants with a sticky barrier around plant stems first.
source: RAB Extension Manual; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my watermelon are are stunted and the leaves are drying out. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Yellowing leaves that wilt during the day and internal stem browning indicate Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum). Once a plant shows symptoms, it cannot be saved. (1) Uproot and burn the affected plant with its root ball — do NOT compost. (2) Drench the planting hole with Trichoderma viride (10 g/L) + lime (50 g/hole). (3) Do NOT plant susceptible crops in that spot for 3-4 years — rotate with maize or rice. (4) Solarize the soil during the hottest months. (5) Use resistant varieties (FHIA series for banana). (6) Always use tissue-culture plantlets or certified disease-free suckers for new plantings — the fungus persists in infected planting material.
source: ICIPE Integrated Pest Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my cashew are are turning yellow with dark spots. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: Dark, sunken lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit indicate anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.). (1) Remove and destroy all infected plant parts — do NOT compost them. (2) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L or mancozeb at 2.5 g/L every 10-14 days, starting at flowering. (3) Prune to improve air circulation and reduce humidity. (4) Apply 2-3 cm of organic mulch to prevent rain splash. (5) For the next season, use certified disease-free seed and practice 3-year crop rotation with cereals. Pre-harvest interval: 7-14 days depending on the product.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Hello. The leaves on my cassava are are turning yellow with dark spots. I need urgent advice before I lose the whole crop.
answer: This is cassava whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Do NOT spray broad-spectrum insecticides — they kill natural enemies like Encarsia wasps and make outbreaks worse. Instead: (1) Spray insecticidal soap or 0.5% neem oil solution every 7 days for 3 weeks. (2) Remove and burn heavily infested leaves. (3) Plant maize or sorghum as barrier crops between cassava rows to disrupt whitefly movement. (4) Use yellow sticky traps (1 per 10 m²). If infestation persists, apply imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L as a LAST resort, observing a 14-day pre-harvest interval. Wash hands and produce after application.
source: CIMMYT Southern Africa Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Good morning. My maize plants have small insects clustered on them. I've tried a few things but it's getting worse. What should I do?
answer: The small holes and shredded young leaves indicate fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda). Act immediately — one larva can destroy 3 whorls. (1) Hand-pick and crush egg masses (fuzzy white patches) and visible larvae, especially at dawn or dusk. (2) Apply a 5% neem seed extract (50 g ground neem seed per litre of water, soak 12 hrs, strain) into the whorl of each plant — the larvae ingest it and stop feeding within hours. (3) In maize, add dry sand or ash (1 pinch per whorl) — it desiccates the larvae. (4) As a last resort, apply emamectin benzoate at 0.4 ml/L or spinosad at 0.3 ml/L. (5) Push-pull: plant Desmodium between rows to repel moths and Napier grass around fields to trap them. Pre-harvest interval for spinosad: 3 days.
source: NARO Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo tomato m nwere obere ahụhụ na akwụkwọ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Concentric ring spots on older leaves indicate early blight (Alternaria solani). (1) Remove affected lower leaves and burn them. (2) Spray chlorothalonil at 2 g/L or mancozeb at 2.5 g/L every 7-10 days. (3) Apply 2-3 cm of organic mulch to prevent soil splash. (4) Ensure adequate potassium — apply 100 kg/ha muriate of potash. (5) Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (maize, beans) for 2-3 years. (6) Stake plants to keep foliage off the ground. Pre-harvest interval: chlorothalonil 7 days.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo rice m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Oval brown spots on leaves indicate brown spot (Cochliobolus miyabeanus), often associated with nutrient deficiency, especially silicon. (1) Apply potassium silicate at 2 ml/L foliar spray — this strengthens leaf cell walls. (2) Apply balanced NPK (15-15-15) at 200 kg/ha if the crop appears yellowish overall. (3) Spray propiconazole at 1 ml/L if spots cover >10% of leaf area. (4) Avoid water stress — maintain 2-5 cm standing water. (5) For the next season, incorporate rice husks into the soil to increase silicon availability.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Daalunu. cowpea m nwere obere ahụhụ na akwụkwọ. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Stunted growth, yellowing, swollen root galls (knots), and wilting despite moist soil indicate root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.). (1) There is no curative chemical treatment. (2) Incorporate fresh neem leaves or neem cake at 500 kg/ha into the soil 2 weeks before the next planting. (3) Solarize the soil with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks. (4) Plant marigold (Tagetes erecta) as a trap crop — its roots release natural nematicides. (5) Rotate with maize, sorghum, or millet for 2-3 seasons — these are non-hosts. (6) Apply well-composted manure at 5 t/ha; the microbial activity suppresses nematodes.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo mango m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Small, immobile brown or white bumps on stems and leaf veins are scale insects. (1) Scrape off light infestations with a soft brush and soapy water. (2) Apply horticultural mineral oil at 2% (20 ml/L) ensuring thorough coverage — it smothers the scales. (3) Prune heavily infested branches and burn them. (4) Apply imidacloprid as a soil drench for persistent infestation (0.5 ml/L). (5) Encourage natural enemies: ladybirds and parasitic wasps. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill these beneficial insects. (6) Check nursery seedlings for scale BEFORE planting.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo groundnut m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Aflatoxin contamination is caused by Aspergillus fungi and is a serious food safety risk — it can cause liver disease. Prevention is everything: (1) Harvest at the right maturity — do NOT delay harvest, especially if rains are expected. (2) Dry produce rapidly and thoroughly to below 13% moisture. Use raised drying racks, not bare ground. (3) Store in hermetic (airtight) bags — PICS bags or metal silos — away from heat and moisture. (4) Sort and discard any grains that are discoloured, shriveled, or moldy BEFORE storage. (5) Apply Aflasafe (biocontrol product available in Nigeria, Kenya) at 10 kg/ha 2-3 weeks before flowering. (6) NEVER feed mouldy grain to livestock.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

answer: Dark, sunken lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit indicate anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.). (1) Remove and destroy all infected plant parts — do NOT compost them. (2) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L or mancozeb at 2.5 g/L every 10-14 days, starting at flowering. (3) Prune to improve air circulation and reduce humidity. question: Daalunu. cocoa m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Sunken, black lesions on young shoots and pods indicate mirids/capsids (Sahlbergella singularis). (1) Spray imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L OR bifenthrin at 1 ml/L, targeting the canopy thoroughly. (2) Remove and burn heavily damaged shoots and pods. (3) Maintain adequate canopy shade — mirids prefer open, exposed canopies. (4) Avoid excessive pruning that exposes the tree interior. (5) Monitor weekly with a beating tray or by tapping branches over a white cloth to count insects. Treat when you find >4 mirids per 10 taps.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Daalunu. plantain m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Holes at the base of the pseudostem and wilting plants indicate banana/plantain weevil borer (Cosmopolites sordidus). (1) Set up pseudostem traps: cut a 30 cm piece of harvested stem, split it lengthwise, and place it cut-side down near the plant. Check and destroy trapped weevils every 2 days. (2) Apply neem cake at 100 g per plant around the base. (3) Remove old, harvested stems at ground level — they are breeding sites. (4) For heavy infestation, drench the soil around the base with chlorpyrifos at 2 ml/L (wear gloves and avoid runoff into water sources). (5) Use clean, weevil-free suckers for the next planting.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo sorghum m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Small pink-purple flowering weeds attached to the roots of your sorghum are Striga (witchweed). Each plant produces 50,000+ seeds that persist in soil for 15+ years. (1) Hand-pull ALL Striga plants BEFORE they flower — pull and burn them. (2) Do NOT plant sorghum in the same field next season — rotate with groundnut or cowpea which trigger Striga seed germination but are not parasitised ('suicidal germination'). (3) Apply imazapyr-resistant maize varieties (StrigAway / IR-maize) coated with herbicide at planting. (4) Apply 2 t/ha of well-composted farmyard manure — it improves soil fertility and reduces Striga emergence. (5) Deep-plough after harvest to bury seeds below the germination zone.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo banana m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Upright, crowded leaves with a 'bunchy' appearance and dark green streaking on petioles indicate Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV) transmitted by the banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa). There is NO cure. (1) Uproot and destroy the entire plant including the corm — bury or burn it. (2) Control the aphid vector by spraying imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L on all surrounding plants. (3) Never use suckers from an affected field for new plantings. (4) Use tissue-culture plantlets — they are guaranteed virus-free. (5) Contact your agricultural extension office to report BBTV — it is a notifiable disease in most countries. (6) Quarantine any new planting material for 4 weeks.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo sweet potato m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Distorted, mottled leaves and stunted growth on sweet potato indicate a viral infection, often transmitted by aphids or whiteflies. (1) Remove and destroy affected plants — viruses cannot be cured. (2) Control the insect vectors with neem oil (5 ml/L) or imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L. (3) Use only certified virus-free planting material (vine cuttings or slips). (4) Remove weeds (especially morning glory and other Ipomoea species) that harbour the virus. (5) Plant a barrier crop (maize or sorghum) to disrupt insect movement into the field. (6) Wash hands and tools before handling healthy plants.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Daalunu. onion m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Soft, rotting bulb base with white fungal growth indicates basal rot (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae). (1) Remove and destroy affected plants — do NOT store bulbs from infected rows. (2) Treat seed bulbs with Trichoderma viride (10 g/kg seed) before planting. (3) Avoid injury to bulbs during weeding. (4) Harvest when 50% of tops have fallen and cure bulbs in the sun for 7-10 days. (5) Store in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place. (6) Rotate away from alliums for 4 years.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Daalunu. pepper m nwere obere ahụhụ na akwụkwọ. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Brown spots on pepper leaves indicate leaf spot disease (Cercospora / Alternaria spp.). (1) Remove and destroy affected leaves. (2) Spray mancozeb at 2.5 g/L OR copper oxychloride at 3 g/L every 10-14 days. (3) Improve air circulation through wider spacing. (4) Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet. (5) Apply well-rotted compost at 2 t/ha to boost plant immunity. (6) Rotate with non-host crops for 2 seasons.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Daalunu. okra m nwere obere ahụhụ na akwụkwọ. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: White powdery coating on leaves indicates powdery mildew (Erysiphales). It reduces photosynthesis and weakens plants. (1) Spray sulfur-based fungicide (micronized sulfur at 3 g/L) or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) every 7 days. (2) Improve air circulation by wider spacing and removing excess foliage. (3) Avoid overhead irrigation — water at the base of plants. (4) Spray a solution of 1 part milk to 9 parts water — milk proteins have antifungal properties effective against powdery mildew. Apply weekly. (5) Remove and burn heavily infected leaves. Pre-harvest interval for sulfur: 1 day.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Daalunu. millet m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Holes in stems and 'dead hearts' (withered central shoot) indicate stem borers (Busseola fusca / Chilo partellus). (1) Pull out and destroy dead heart plants — larvae inside can spread to healthy plants. (2) Apply crushed neem leaves (1 kg/10 L water, steep 24 hours) into the leaf whorl — repeat weekly. (3) Apply carbofuran 3G granules at 0.75 kg a.i./ha into the whorl at knee-height stage. (4) After harvest, cut stubble to ground level and bury or burn crop residues to kill overwintering larvae. (5) Rotate with legumes (cowpea, groundnut) to break the pest cycle.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo coffee m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Dark, sunken lesions on green berries that turn black and drop indicate Coffee Berry Disease (Colletotrichum kahawae). (1) Spray copper oxychloride at 5 g/L on the developing berries at 4, 8, and 12 weeks after flowering. (2) Prune to maintain an open canopy — this reduces humidity and spore dispersal. (3) Strip and burn all mummified berries remaining on branches after harvest. (4) Apply 2 t/ha of well-rotted compost to improve tree vigour. (5) Plant resistant varieties: Ruiru 11 or Batian (available in Kenya). Pre-harvest interval for copper: 21 days.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo tea m nwere obere ahụhụ na akwụkwọ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Soft, foul-smelling roots indicate root rot caused by soil fungi (Pythium/Phytophthora). (1) Stop watering immediately — wet soil accelerates the rot. (2) Improve drainage by creating raised beds 30 cm high. (3) Remove and destroy all affected plants. (4) Drench the remaining soil with Trichoderma viride at 2.5 kg/ha mixed with 50 kg of well-rotted compost. (5) For the next planting season, solarize the soil by covering beds with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks during the hottest months. (6) Rotate tea with maize or sorghum for at least 2 seasons before replanting.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo oil palm m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Yellowing patterns on oil palm indicate nutrient deficiency. (1) For nitrogen deficiency (uniform yellowing of older leaves): apply urea at 1-2 kg per tree per year, split into 2 applications. (2) For potassium deficiency (orange spotting on older leaves): apply muriate of potash at 2-3 kg per tree per year. (3) For magnesium deficiency (yellowing between veins of older leaves): apply kieserite at 0.5-1 kg per tree. (4) Apply empty fruit bunch (EFB) mulch at 60 t/ha around palms — it slowly releases nutrients. (5) Conduct a leaf analysis (take leaf #17 from 20 palms) to confirm which nutrients are deficient before large-scale fertiliser application.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

answer: Small black or pale green insects clustered on stems and young growth are aphids. They suck sap and can transmit viruses. question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo cabbage m nwere obere ahụhụ na akwụkwọ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: V-shaped yellow lesions at leaf margins with blackened veins indicate black rot (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris). (1) Remove and destroy affected plants — the bacteria spread through water. (2) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L to protect remaining plants. (3) Use hot-water treated seed (50°C for 25 minutes) for the next planting. (4) Never work in the field when plants are wet. (5) Rotate with non-crucifer crops (maize, cowpea) for 3-4 years. (6) Control weeds in the cabbage family (wild mustard, shepherd's purse) that harbour the bacteria.
source: IITA Crop Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo cassava m nwere obere ahụhụ na akwụkwọ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Brown leaf spots on cassava are caused by Cercospora fungi. (1) Remove severely infected lower leaves and burn them. (2) Spray mancozeb (2 g/L of water) or copper oxychloride (3 g/L) every 10-14 days during wet weather. (3) Improve air circulation by widening plant spacing to 1 m × 1 m. (4) Apply mulch to prevent rain splash that spreads spores. (5) For the next crop, choose a well-drained field and apply 2 t/ha of well-rotted compost to strengthen plant resistance. Fungicide pre-harvest interval: minimum 21 days.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo maize m nwere obere ahụhụ na akwụkwọ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Chlorotic streaks following leaf veins indicate Maize Streak Virus transmitted by leafhoppers (Cicadulina spp.). There is no cure. (1) Remove and destroy all affected plants immediately. (2) Plant early at the onset of rains to avoid peak leafhopper populations. (3) Use streak-resistant hybrids: ZM 623, SC 627, or WH 505. (4) Do not plant maize near irrigated vegetable fields, which harbor leafhoppers year-round. (5) Apply carbofuran granules at 1.5 kg a.i./ha to the soil at planting to control early-season vectors. (6) Save seed only from completely disease-free plants.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo tomato m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Dark, leathery rot at the blossom end of the fruit is blossom end rot — NOT a disease but a calcium disorder caused by irregular watering. (1) Water consistently — apply 25-30 mm of water per week, split across 2-3 sessions. Do NOT let the soil dry out then flood. (2) Apply gypsum (calcium sulfate) at 100 kg/ha before the next planting. (3) For immediate correction, spray calcium chloride (5 g/L) on the leaves and developing fruit every 5 days for 3 applications. (4) Mulch heavily (5 cm) to maintain even soil moisture. (5) Avoid excessive nitrogen fertiliser which causes rapid growth and calcium dilution. Remove affected fruit so the plant redirects energy to healthy ones.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo rice m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Bronze-orange discolouration of older leaves ("bronzing") indicates iron toxicity, common in waterlogged, acidic soils. (1) Drain the field for 3-5 days to aerate the soil — this allows iron to precipitate out of the soil solution. (2) Apply lime (2-4 t/ha) to raise soil pH above 5.0. (3) Use NPK 15-15-15 fertiliser rather than single-nutrient fertilisers — potassium helps reduce iron uptake. (4) Plant tolerant varieties: NERICA-L series or TOX 4004. (5) In the next season, avoid continuous flooding of young seedlings; use alternate wetting and drying irrigation.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo cowpea m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Small black or pale green insects clustered on stems and young growth are aphids. They suck sap and can transmit viruses. (1) Spray insecticidal soap (5 ml liquid soap in 1 L water) directly on the insects every 3 days. (2) Strong water spray can dislodge light infestations. (3) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L. (4) Encourage natural enemies: ladybirds (ladybugs), lacewings, and hoverflies — plant marigold or coriander near cowpea to attract them. question: Daalunu. groundnut m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: Brown spots on groundnut leaves indicate leaf spot disease (Cercospora / Alternaria spp.). (1) Remove and destroy affected leaves. (2) Spray mancozeb at 2.5 g/L OR copper oxychloride at 3 g/L every 10-14 days. (3) Improve air circulation through wider spacing. (4) Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet. (5) Apply well-rotted compost at 2 t/ha to boost plant immunity. (6) Rotate with non-host crops for 2 seasons.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Daalunu. yam m anaghị eto nke ọma, akwukwo na-akpọnwụ. Gini ka m ga-eme?
answer: The yellow-green leaf pattern you describe is Cassava Mosaic Disease caused by geminiviruses transmitted by whiteflies. There is no chemical cure. (1) Uproot and burn ALL affected plants immediately — do NOT use them as planting material. (2) Use certified mosaic-resistant varieties: TME 419, TMS 30572, or IITA-TMS-I011412. (3) Plant stakes at the recommended spacing of 1 m × 1 m. (4) Avoid recycling stakes from infected fields. (5) Intercrop with maize or cowpea to reduce whitefly populations. Contact your nearest IITA or NRCRI extension office for free resistant planting material.
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo cocoa m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Holes in pods with frass (insect droppings) indicate pod borer (Maruca vitrata / Helicoverpa armigera). (1) Hand-pick visible caterpillars at dawn. (2) Spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) at 2 g/L in the evening — it degrades in sunlight. (3) Apply neem seed kernel extract (50 g/L, soak 12 hrs, strain) weekly. (4) Plant early-maturing varieties to escape peak pest pressure. (5) Install pheromone traps (1 per 0.1 ha) to monitor moth flights. (6) After harvest, deep-plough (20-25 cm) to expose pupae to sunlight and birds. Pre-harvest interval for Bt: 0 days (safe up to harvest day).
source: NRCRI Extension Bulletin; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nnukwu m, akwukwo plantain m na-acha odo odo na ntụpọ ojii. Biko nyere m aka.
answer: Dark brown streaks that enlarge to black spots on leaves indicate Black Sigatoka (Mycosphaerella fijiensis). This disease can reduce yield by 50%+. (1) Remove and destroy all heavily infected leaves — do NOT leave them on the ground. (2) Spray propiconazole at 1 ml/L OR difenoconazole at 0.5 ml/L every 14-21 days during the rainy season. ALTERNATE fungicides to prevent resistance. (3) Improve drainage — standing water increases spore production. (4) Reduce planting density for better airflow (standard: 1,700 plants/ha; reduce to 1,400 if disease is severe). (5) De-leaf weekly, leaving only 8-10 functional leaves per plant.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Witamwo. banana yakwa ndikuaga wega, mahuti ni kuuma. Ndingakora atia?
answer: Yellowing leaves that wilt during the day and internal stem browning indicate Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum). Once a plant shows symptoms, it cannot be saved. (1) Uproot and burn the affected plant with its root ball — do NOT compost. (2) Drench the planting hole with Trichoderma viride (10 g/L) + lime (50 g/hole). (3) Do NOT plant susceptible crops in that spot for 3-4 years — rotate with maize or rice. (4) Solarize the soil during the hottest months. (5) Use resistant varieties (FHIA series for banana). (6) Always use tissue-culture plantlets or certified disease-free suckers for new plantings — the fungus persists in infected planting material.
source: ICIPE Integrated Pest Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nina thina na sweet potato. Mahuti make irina tuthoni tuthoni thiini wa mahuti. Ndataithie.
answer: Stunted growth, yellowing, swollen root galls (knots), and wilting despite moist soil indicate root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.). (1) There is no curative chemical treatment. (2) Incorporate fresh neem leaves or neem cake at 500 kg/ha into the soil 2 weeks before the next planting. (3) Solarize the soil with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks. (4) Plant marigold (Tagetes erecta) as a trap crop — its roots release natural nematicides. (5) Rotate with maize, sorghum, or millet for 2-3 seasons — these are non-hosts. question: Witamwo. onion yakwa irina tuthoni tuthoni thiini wa mahuti. Ndingakora atia?
answer: Silvery streaks on leaves and distorted young growth indicate thrips. (1) Spray spinosad at 0.3 ml/L or neem oil at 5 ml/L every 5 days. (2) Use blue sticky traps (thrips are more attracted to blue than yellow), 1 trap per 5 m². (3) Remove weeds from around the field — they serve as alternative hosts. (4) Maintain adequate soil moisture — drought stressed plants are more vulnerable. (5) For heavy infestations, apply imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L as a soil drench. Pre-harvest interval: spinosad 3 days.

question: Witamwo. pepper yakwa ndikuaga wega, mahuti ni kuuma. Ndingakora atia?
answer: Sudden wilting of green plants with no leaf yellowing indicates bacterial wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum). Cut the stem — if it oozes a milky bacterial stream in water, it's confirmed. There is NO chemical cure. (1) Uproot and burn affected plants. (2) Raise soil pH to 6.0-6.5 by applying lime (2 t/ha). (3) Graft pepper onto resistant rootstocks (e.g., EG 203 eggplant rootstock). (4) Rotate with maize or sorghum for 3-4 years — the bacteria survive in soil. (5) Solarize soil before the next planting. (6) Never plant pepper after tomato, potato, or eggplant.

question: Witamwo. okra yakwa ni kuuga njano na nduithia njeru. Ndingakora atia?
answer: Holes in developing pods with black frass indicate fruit borer (Earias spp. / Helicoverpa armigera). (1) Hand-pick caterpillars at dawn. (2) Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) at 2 g/L in the evening every 7 days. (3) Apply neem seed kernel extract (50 g/L). (4) Install pheromone traps at 5 traps/ha. (5) Plant trap crop: maize rows around okra to attract borers away. (6) Remove crop residues after harvest and deep-plough.
source: KALRO Diagnostic Manual; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Witamwo. millet yakwa ni kuuga njano na nduithia njeru. Ndingakora atia?
answer: Damaged grain heads with small holes and frass indicate head miner / head bug (various species). (1) Spray lambda-cyhalothrin at 1 ml/L at 50% flowering and repeat after 10 days. (2) Plant early and uniformly to synchronize flowering. (3) Use pheromone traps to time sprays. (4) Remove alternative grass hosts from field borders. (5) Apply neem seed kernel extract (50 g/L) if synthetic insecticides are unavailable. Pre-harvest interval: lambda-cyhalothrin 14 days.
source: ICIPE Integrated Pest Management Guide; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Witamwo. oil palm yakwa irina tuthoni tuthoni thiini wa mahuti. Ndingakora atia?
answer: Brown spots on oil palm leaves indicate leaf spot disease (Cercospora / Alternaria spp.). (1) Remove and destroy affected leaves. (2) Spray mancozeb at 2.5 g/L OR copper oxychloride at 3 g/L every 10-14 days. (3) Improve air circulation through wider spacing. (4) Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet. question: Nina thina na amaranth. Mahuti make ndikuaga wega, mahuti ni kuuma. Ndataithie.
answer: White powdery coating on leaves indicates powdery mildew (Erysiphales). It reduces photosynthesis and weakens plants. (1) Spray sulfur-based fungicide (micronized sulfur at 3 g/L) or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) every 7 days. (2) Improve air circulation by wider spacing and removing excess foliage. (3) Avoid overhead irrigation — water at the base of plants. (4) Spray a solution of 1 part milk to 9 parts water — milk proteins have antifungal properties effective against powdery mildew. Apply weekly. (5) Remove and burn heavily infected leaves. Pre-harvest interval for sulfur: 1 day.

question: Nina thina na cabbage. Mahuti make ni kuuga njano na nduithia njeru. Ndataithie.
answer: V-shaped yellow lesions at leaf margins with blackened veins indicate black rot (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris). (1) Remove and destroy affected plants — the bacteria spread through water. (2) Spray copper oxychloride at 3 g/L to protect remaining plants. question: Nina thina na watermelon. Mahuti make irina tuthoni tuthoni thiini wa mahuti. Ndataithie.
answer: Small black or pale green insects clustered on stems and young growth are aphids. They suck sap and can transmit viruses. (1) Spray insecticidal soap (5 ml liquid soap in 1 L water) directly on the insects every 3 days. (2) Strong water spray can dislodge light infestations. (3) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L. (4) Encourage natural enemies: ladybirds (ladybugs), lacewings, and hoverflies — plant marigold or coriander near watermelon to attract them. (5) If infestation is severe and ants are present (ants farm aphids), apply imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/L. Remove ants with a sticky barrier around plant stems first.

question: Nina thina na cashew. Mahuti make irina tuthoni tuthoni thiini wa mahuti. Ndataithie.
answer: Brown, necrotic spots on leaves and dieback of young shoots indicate Tea Mosquito Bug (Helopeltis spp.). (1) Spray lambda-cyhalothrin at 1 ml/L OR quinalphos at 2 ml/L, targeting the new flush. (2) Maintain adequate shade (50-60%) — open areas suffer more damage. (3) Remove alternative host plants (especially guava, cashew) near the tea field. (4) Prune affected shoots and burn them. (5) Apply neem oil at 5 ml/L as a repellent. Pre-harvest interval (plucking): lambda-cyhalothrin 7 days.

question: Nina thina na cassava. Mahuti make irina tuthoni tuthoni thiini wa mahuti. Ndataithie.
answer: Soft, foul-smelling roots indicate root rot caused by soil fungi (Pythium/Phytophthora). (1) Stop watering immediately — wet soil accelerates the rot. (2) Improve drainage by creating raised beds 30 cm high. (3) Remove and destroy all affected plants. (4) Drench the remaining soil with Trichoderma viride at 2.5 kg/ha mixed with 50 kg of well-rotted compost. (5) For the next planting season, solarize the soil by covering beds with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks during the hottest months. (6) Rotate cassava with maize or sorghum for at least 2 seasons before replanting.

question: Witamwo. maize yakwa ni kuuga njano na nduithia njeru. Ndingakora atia?
answer: Yellowing of lower leaves (starting at the tip and moving inward in a V shape on maize) indicates nitrogen deficiency. (1) Apply urea (46-0-0) at the rate of 50 kg/ha — split into two doses: half at 3 weeks after planting, half at 6 weeks. Place fertiliser in a band 5 cm from the plant and 3 cm deep — do NOT leave it on the soil surface. (2) Alternatively, apply well-composted poultry manure at 5 t/ha. (3) Intercrop with cowpea or groundnut — they fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil for your maize. (4) Do NOT apply urea when the soil is dry; wait until after rainfall or irrigate lightly.
source: FAO Agricultural Guidelines, 2024; reviewed agricultural literature

question: Nina thina na tomato. Mahuti make ni kuuga njano na nduithia njeru. Ndataithie.
answer: Dark, leathery rot at the blossom end of the fruit is blossom end rot — NOT a disease but a calcium disorder caused by irregular watering. (1) Water consistently — apply 25-30 mm of water per week, split across 2-3 sessions. Do NOT let the soil dry out then flood. (2) Apply gypsum (calcium sulfate) at 100 kg/ha before the next planting. (3) For immediate correction, spray calcium chloride (5 g/L) on the leaves and developing fruit every 5 days for 3 applications. (4) Mulch heavily (5 cm) to maintain even soil moisture. (5) Avoid excessive nitrogen fertiliser which causes rapid growth and calcium dilution. Remove affected fruit so the plant redirects energy to healthy ones.
